notes:
AC Basics

  • $v = v_0\sin\omega t$, $i = i_0\sin(\omega t+\phi)$. RMS value: $v_{rms}=v_0/\sqrt2$, $i_{rms}=i_0/\sqrt2$ (for sinusoidal ac); average over a full cycle is zero, average of $\sin^2$ over a cycle is $1/2$.
  • AC voltmeters/ammeters read rms values. Power: $P_{avg} = v_{rms}i_{rms}\cos\phi$ ($\cos\phi$ = power factor).

Circuit Elements

ElementReactanceCurrent vs voltagePower factor
Resistor $R$$R$in phase1
Inductor $L$$X_L=\omega L$current lags by $90^\circ$0
Capacitor $C$$X_C=1/\omega C$current leads by $90^\circ$0

Series LCR Circuit

  • Impedance $Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$; $\tan\phi = \dfrac{X_L-X_C}{R}$.
  • Resonance: $X_L=X_C \Rightarrow \omega_0 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$; at resonance $Z=R$ (minimum), current is maximum, circuit behaves purely resistive, power factor $=1$.
  • Sharpness of resonance measured by Q-factor: $Q = \dfrac{\omega_0L}{R} = \dfrac1R\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{C}} = \dfrac{\omega_0}{\text{bandwidth}}$.
  • Power dissipated only in $R$: $P = i_{rms}^2R = v_{rms}i_{rms}\cos\phi$. Purely inductive/capacitive circuits: average power over a cycle is zero — called wattless current.

Transformer

  • $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p} = \dfrac{I_p}{I_s}$ (ideal, no losses). Step-up: $N_s>N_p$, increases voltage decreases current. Step-down: opposite.
  • Losses: copper loss ($I^2R$ in windings, reduced by thick wire), eddy current loss (reduced by lamination), hysteresis loss (reduced by soft iron core), flux leakage.
  • Long-distance transmission uses high voltage, low current (via step-up transformers) to minimise $I^2R$ line losses.

LC Oscillations

  • Charged capacitor connected to inductor: energy oscillates between electric ($\dfrac{Q^2}{2C}$) and magnetic ($\dfrac12LI^2$) forms, analogous to SHM; angular frequency $\omega=1/\sqrt{LC}$, undamped only in the ideal (resistance-free) case.

Exam tip

KCET typically asks 2–3 questions: an rms/peak-value or power-factor numerical, a resonance frequency ($\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}$) calculation, and a transformer turns-ratio problem. Remember pure L or C draws current but consumes zero average power (wattless).

questions.q: The peak value of an alternating current is 10 A. Its rms value is
questions.trick: $i_{rms}=i_0/\sqrt2\approx0.707\,i_0$ — memorise the 0.707 factor directly.

questions.q: An ac source of rms voltage 220 V is connected to a pure resistor of 100 $\Omega$. The average power dissipated is
questions.trick: Pure resistor: $P=V_{rms}^2/R$, use rms voltage directly, no $\cos\phi$ needed.

questions.q: In a purely inductive ac circuit, the current
questions.explanation: For an inductor, $V=L\,di/dt$ makes the current lag the voltage by $90^\circ$ ('ELI').
questions.trick: Remember 'ELI': in an inductor, EMF leads current — current LAGS by 90°.

questions.q: In a purely capacitive ac circuit, the average power consumed over a full cycle is
questions.explanation: Power factor $\cos\phi = \cos90^\circ = 0$ for a pure capacitor, so average power over a cycle is zero (wattless current).
questions.trick: Pure C or pure L: power factor is zero, so average power is always zero.

questions.q: The reactance of an inductor of 0.5 H at a frequency of 50 Hz is
questions.explanation: $X_L = \omega L = 2\pi fL = 2\pi\times50\times0.5 = 157\,\Omega$.
questions.trick: $X_L=2\pi fL$ — plug in directly, don't forget the $2\pi$.

questions.q: The capacitive reactance of a 10 $\mu$F capacitor at 50 Hz is approximately
questions.explanation: $X_C = 1/(2\pi fC) = 1/(2\pi\times50\times10\times10^{-6}) = 1/(3.14\times10^{-3}) \approx 318\,\Omega$.
questions.trick: $X_C=1/(2\pi fC)$ — reciprocal relation, larger $C$ means smaller $X_C$.

questions.q: A series LCR circuit has $R=30\,\Omega$, $X_L=70\,\Omega$, $X_C=30\,\Omega$. The impedance of the circuit is
questions.trick: $Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$ — subtract reactances first, then Pythagoras.

questions.q: At resonance, a series LCR circuit behaves as
questions.explanation: At resonance $X_L=X_C$, so $Z=R$ (minimum possible value), the circuit is purely resistive and current is maximum.
questions.trick: Resonance: $Z=R$ minimum, current maximum, purely resistive — the three facts to recall.

questions.q: The resonant frequency of a series LCR circuit with $L=1$ H and $C=1\,\mu$F is nearly
questions.explanation: $f_0 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{1\times10^{-6}}} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\times10^{-3}} \approx 159$ Hz.
questions.trick: $f_0=1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$ — same shape as $\omega_0$, just divide by $2\pi$.

questions.q: A step-down transformer converts 220 V to 22 V. If the primary has 1000 turns, the number of turns in the secondary is
questions.explanation: $N_s/N_p = V_s/V_p \Rightarrow N_s = 1000\times(22/220) = 100$.
questions.trick: $N_s/N_p=V_s/V_p$ — turns ratio equals voltage ratio directly.

questions.q: An ideal transformer steps up voltage from 100 V to 1000 V. If the primary current is 10 A, the secondary current is
questions.explanation: For an ideal transformer, input power = output power: $V_pI_p = V_sI_s \Rightarrow I_s = 100\times10/1000 = 1$ A.
questions.trick: Ideal transformer: $V_pI_p=V_sI_s$ — power conserved, so current ratio is inverse of voltage ratio.

questions.q: Eddy current losses in a transformer core are reduced by
questions.explanation: Laminating the core with thin, mutually insulated sheets restricts the paths available for eddy currents, reducing heating losses.
questions.trick: Eddy current fix in transformers: laminated core, same trick as in motors/generators.

questions.q: In a series LCR circuit at resonance, the power factor is
questions.explanation: At resonance the circuit is purely resistive ($\phi=0$), so $\cos\phi = 1$.
questions.trick: At resonance power factor is always exactly 1 — purely resistive behaviour.

questions.q: High voltage is used for long-distance transmission of electric power mainly to
options: reduce $I^2R$ power loss in transmission lines by lowering the current
increase the current for better heating
increase the resistance of the lines
questions.explanation: For fixed power $P=VI$, raising $V$ lowers $I$; since line loss $=I^2R$, a lower current drastically cuts losses over long cables.
questions.trick: High voltage transmission: $P=VI$ fixed, so higher $V$ means lower $I$, and loss $\propto I^2$.

questions.q: A choke coil is preferred over a resistor to control current in an ac circuit because
options: a choke works only in dc circuits
a choke consumes negligible average power (nearly wattless) while limiting current
a choke has more resistance than a resistor
questions.explanation: An ideal inductor (choke) has power factor $\approx 0$, so it limits ac current via reactance while dissipating almost no power, unlike a resistor which wastes energy as heat.
questions.trick: Choke coil: reactance limits current with near-zero power loss — that's the whole advantage over a resistor.

questions.q: In an LC oscillation circuit (no resistance), when all the energy is stored in the capacitor, the current in the circuit is
questions.explanation: Energy oscillates between $C$ (as $Q^2/2C$) and $L$ (as $LI^2/2$); when all energy is electrical (in $C$), the magnetic energy and hence current is zero.
questions.trick: LC oscillation: all energy in C means zero magnetic energy, so current is exactly zero.

questions.q: The Q-factor of a series LCR resonant circuit is given by
questions.explanation: $Q = \omega_0L/R = \dfrac1R\sqrt{L/C}$; a higher $Q$ means a sharper resonance curve.
questions.trick: $Q=\frac1R\sqrt{L/C}$ — higher $Q$ means sharper resonance peak.

questions.q: A 100 V, 50 Hz ac source is connected to a series combination of $R=40\,\Omega$ and $X_L=30\,\Omega$ (no capacitor). The current in the circuit is
questions.trick: RL circuit (no C): $Z=\sqrt{R^2+X_L^2}$ then $I=V/Z$ — standard two-step.

questions.q: For a series RL ac circuit with $R=40\,\Omega$ and $X_L=30\,\Omega$ (so $Z=50\,\Omega$), the power factor is
questions.trick: Power factor $=R/Z$ always — the resistive fraction of total impedance.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about a transformer is correct?
options: It can step up or step down dc voltage efficiently
It works on both ac and dc equally well
It works only on ac, based on mutual induction between primary and secondary coils
questions.explanation: A transformer relies on a continuously changing flux linking the primary and secondary coils (mutual induction), which requires alternating current; it cannot step dc voltage and never creates extra power (ideal efficiency = 100%, real transformers have losses).
questions.trick: Transformer works ONLY on ac — needs continuously changing flux via mutual induction.

questions.q: For a sinusoidal alternating current $i=i_0\sin\omega t$, the average value taken over one half cycle is
questions.explanation: Averaging $i_0\sin\omega t$ over a half cycle gives $i_{avg}=\dfrac{2i_0}{\pi}\approx0.637i_0$, while the average over a full cycle is zero.
questions.trick: Half-cycle average of sine is $2i_0/\pi\approx0.637i_0$ — different from rms's 0.707.

questions.q: An ac source of rms voltage 100 V is connected in series with a resistor $R=30\,\Omega$ and a capacitor with $X_C=40\,\Omega$. The rms current in the circuit is
questions.trick: RC circuit: $Z=\sqrt{R^2+X_C^2}$, same Pythagoras pattern as RL, just swap $X_L$ for $X_C$.

questions.q: A series RC circuit with $R=30\,\Omega$ and $X_C=40\,\Omega$ is connected to an ac source. The power factor and the phase relation between current and voltage are
questions.explanation: $\cos\phi=R/Z=30/50=0.6$; in a series RC circuit, the current leads the applied voltage.
questions.trick: In RC circuits, current always LEADS the voltage — opposite phase behaviour to RL.

questions.q: A series LCR circuit has $R=30\,\Omega$, $X_L=90\,\Omega$, $X_C=50\,\Omega$. The impedance and the nature of the circuit are
questions.explanation: $Z=\sqrt{30^2+(90-50)^2}=\sqrt{900+1600}=50\,\Omega$; since $X_L>X_C$, the circuit is net inductive and current lags voltage.
questions.trick: $X_L>X_C$ means net inductive circuit → current lags voltage; check the sign first.

questions.q: At resonance, a parallel LC circuit (tank circuit) has
options: maximum impedance and minimum line current (current magnification in the branches)
impedance independent of L and C
minimum impedance and maximum line current
questions.explanation: Unlike series resonance, a parallel LCR/LC circuit at resonance offers maximum impedance to the source, so the line current drawn is minimum, even though large circulating currents exist in the L and C branches.
questions.trick: Parallel LC (tank) at resonance: impedance is MAXIMUM, current MINIMUM — opposite of series.

questions.q: For a series LCR circuit with $R=10\,\Omega$ and $L=0.5$ H, the bandwidth (difference between the half-power angular frequencies), given by $\Delta\omega=R/L$, is
questions.explanation: $\Delta\omega = R/L = 10/0.5 = 20$ rad/s.
questions.trick: Bandwidth $\Delta\omega=R/L$ — simple ratio, no square roots involved.

questions.q: For a series LCR resonant circuit with resonant angular frequency $\omega_0=1000$ rad/s and bandwidth $\Delta\omega=20$ rad/s, the quality factor $Q$ is
questions.explanation: $Q=\omega_0/\Delta\omega=1000/20=50$; a larger $Q$ means a sharper resonance curve.
questions.trick: $Q=\omega_0/\Delta\omega$ — resonant frequency divided by bandwidth, straightforward.

questions.q: The form factor of a sinusoidal ac (ratio of rms value to average value over half a cycle) is approximately
questions.explanation: Form factor $=\dfrac{i_{rms}}{i_{avg}}=\dfrac{i_0/\sqrt2}{2i_0/\pi}=\dfrac{\pi}{2\sqrt2}\approx1.11$.
questions.trick: Form factor $=\pi/(2\sqrt2)\approx1.11$ — a fixed number worth memorising for sine waves.

questions.q: A transformer has an input power of 2000 W. If the total power loss (copper + iron losses) is 100 W, its efficiency is
questions.explanation: Efficiency $=\dfrac{\text{output}}{\text{input}}\times100=\dfrac{2000-100}{2000}\times100=95\%$.
questions.trick: Transformer efficiency $=(\text{input}-\text{loss})/\text{input}\times100$ — subtract loss from input first.

questions.q: A current that flows in a circuit but whose average power consumption over a cycle is zero (power factor zero) is termed
questions.explanation: In a purely inductive or capacitive circuit, current flows but does no net work over a cycle; such a current is called the wattless (idle) component.
questions.trick: Zero-power-factor current in pure L or C circuits is called wattless (idle) current.

questions.q: The rms value of the mains ac supply is 220 V. Its peak value is approximately
questions.explanation: $V_0=V_{rms}\times\sqrt2=220\times1.414\approx311$ V.
questions.trick: $V_0=V_{rms}\times\sqrt2$ — for 220 V mains this gives the classic 311 V peak.

questions.q: In a series LCR circuit, the phase relationship between the voltage across the inductor ($V_L$) and the voltage across the capacitor ($V_C$) is
options: 180° out of phase (antiphase) with each other
questions.explanation: $V_L$ leads the current by 90° while $V_C$ lags it by 90°, so $V_L$ and $V_C$ are exactly 180° out of phase with each other; their phasors point in opposite directions.
questions.trick: $V_L$ and $V_C$ are always 180° out of phase on the phasor diagram.

questions.q: In an ac circuit, the rms voltage is 100 V, rms current is 2 A, and the phase difference between them is $60^\circ$. The average power consumed is
questions.explanation: $P_{avg}=V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\phi=100\times2\times\cos60^\circ=100\times2\times0.5=100$ W.
questions.trick: $P_{avg}=V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\phi$ — plug in the given phase angle's cosine directly.

questions.q: Hysteresis loss in a transformer core is minimised by using a core material with
options: a narrow hysteresis loop, such as soft iron
high retentivity and coercivity, such as steel
a wide hysteresis loop, such as steel
questions.explanation: A material with a thin (narrow-area) hysteresis loop, like soft iron, dissipates little energy per magnetisation cycle, minimising hysteresis loss.
questions.trick: Narrow hysteresis loop (soft iron) minimises hysteresis loss — same idea as electromagnet cores.

questions.q: An LC circuit has $L=0.01$ H and $C=1\,\mu$F. Its natural angular frequency of oscillation is
questions.trick: $\omega=1/\sqrt{LC}$ — same formula whether asked as $f_0$ or $\omega$, watch which is wanted.

questions.q: At resonance in a series LCR circuit with a high Q-factor, the voltage across the inductor (or capacitor) compared to the applied source voltage is
options: much larger than the source voltage (voltage magnification by factor $Q$)
always less than the source voltage
always equal to the source voltage
questions.explanation: At resonance, $V_L=V_C=Q\times V_{source}$; a high-$Q$ circuit can develop voltages across $L$ and $C$ far exceeding the applied voltage, even though they cancel in the total impedance.
questions.trick: At resonance, $V_L=V_C=Q\times V_{source}$ — high Q means voltage magnification across L, C.

questions.q: In a series LCR circuit driven by a variable-frequency ac source, as the frequency is increased from a low value, the current
options: first increases, reaches a maximum at the resonant frequency, then decreases
questions.explanation: Impedance is minimum ($Z=R$) at resonance, so current is maximum there; it is smaller both below and above resonance, giving a peaked current-frequency graph.
questions.trick: Current-frequency graph always peaks at resonance — rises then falls, never monotonic.

questions.q: At very high frequencies, an inductor behaves approximately like ______ and a capacitor behaves like ______.
options: an open circuit; a short circuit (conducting wire)
a pure emf source; a pure emf source
a short circuit; an open circuit
questions.explanation: $X_L=\omega L\to\infty$ as $\omega\to\infty$ (inductor blocks high-frequency ac), while $X_C=1/\omega C\to0$ (capacitor behaves like a short/wire).
questions.trick: High frequency: inductor $\to$ open circuit ($X_L\to\infty$), capacitor $\to$ short circuit ($X_C\to0$).

questions.q: A series RL circuit with $R=80\,\Omega$ and $X_L=60\,\Omega$ is connected to a 200 V (rms) ac supply. The average power consumed is
questions.trick: $P=VI\cos\phi$ with $\cos\phi=R/Z$ — find $Z$, then $I$, then multiply all three.

questions.q: A series LCR circuit with $R=25\,\Omega$ is connected to a 100 V (rms) ac source at its resonant frequency. The power dissipated is
questions.explanation: At resonance $Z=R$, so $P=V_{rms}^2/R=100^2/25=400$ W.
questions.trick: At resonance $Z=R$, so power is simply $V_{rms}^2/R$ — skip finding $Z$ separately.
